sections.title: Basic Concepts
sections.html:
What is a computer?

  • Computer = machine that accepts input (data + instructions) → processes it → produces useful output.
  • Programmable, multi-use machine: data (raw facts and figures) → information (processed, useful).
  • Made of hardware (physical, tangible parts) + software (programs that run on the hardware).
  • Software = system software + application software.

Benefits of computers

  • Speed: millions of operations per second.
  • Accuracy: correct program + error-free input → correct output.
  • Storage: huge amounts of data in small physical space; fast access.
  • No tiredness: run for days (e.g. weather prediction) without the mistakes a tired human makes.

Uses in everyday life

  • Education: online/distance learning, tutoring, simulation, avatars.
  • Health: telemedicine (doctors treat patients far away via telecommunications), health websites.
  • Government / e-democracy: better services (incl. police), online voting, easier to spread information.
  • Jobs & careers: post résumés, find jobs, start businesses; basic computer skills needed for most jobs.
  • Personal life: safety, home, entertainment, finance, communication, travel, shopping, medical care.

4 basic operations + communications

OperationMeaningDevices
InputWhat goes into the computerKeyboard, mouse, touch screen, scanner, microphone
ProcessingManipulating data into informationCPU + working memory (in the system unit)
StoragePrimary = memory, temporary; Secondary = permanent (hard disk, CD, DVD)Hard disk, tape, memory stick
OutputResults of processing: screen, printout, soundMonitor, printer, speakers
CommunicationsSending and receiving dataModem

Example from the slides: viewers of a TV talent show vote (input) → votes counted (processing) → stored → winners announced (output). This is the information processing cycle.

Some devices do several jobs: printer + scanner + photocopier in one.

CPU (Central Processing Unit)

  • Carries out the basic instructions; manages everything the computer does.
  • ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit): calculations; all arithmetic and logical operations.
  • Control Unit: carries out instructions, controls their order, coordinates all hardware.
  • Main (working) memory works closely with the CPU, holding data and instructions for processing.

Main / primary memory

ROMRAM
Full nameRead Only MemoryRandom Access Memory
Can change?No – stored and used, not modifiedYes – holds data CPU is currently processing
ContainsManufacturer's instructionsCurrent work
Volatile?Non-volatileVolatile (lost when power off)
Analogy–Workbench

Secondary memory (mass / backing storage)

  • Permanent; keeps data when power is off (persistent). Stores data not currently being processed. Analogy: cabinet.
  • Relatively slower and cheaper than main memory.
  • Examples: magnetic tape (common for backup), hard disk, CD/DVD-R, flash drive.
  • Exercise slide: RAM stick = primary; hard disk = secondary.

Peripheral devices

External devices connected to the system unit for input/output.

InputOutputBoth
Keyboard, mouse, digital pen, joystick, scanner, microphoneMonitor, projector, printer, speakersExternal hard drive, digital camcorder, touch screen

Types of computers

Classified by speed, processing capability, price, size. Five basic sizes:

TypeKey facts
SupercomputerFastest, largest; $1M – $350M+; thousands of processors; quadrillions of calculations/sec; census, weather forecasting, aircraft design, scientific projects. Slide: Titan (USA) largest.
MainframeLarge businesses; hundreds of users at once; critical apps (registration, records, reports); $5,000 – $5M; billions of instructions/sec; banks, airlines, insurance, colleges.
WorkstationExpensive, powerful PCs for technical/scientific/professional use: CAD, CAM, maths, engineering, designing cars, drugs, movie special effects; usually networked. Also = a computer connected to a server.
Microcomputer (PC)$500 – $5,000+; stand-alone or networked; desktop, tower, notebook/laptop, netbook, tablet, mobile, PDA, e-reader.
Microcontroller= embedded computer; tiny specialised microprocessor in appliances and cars: microwaves, ovens, blood-pressure monitors, air-bag sensors, MP3 players, cameras.

Servers

  • "Server" describes how a computer is used (could be mainframe, workstation or PC).
  • Central computer holding data (databases) and programs, supplying services to clients.
  • Clients linked by wired/wireless network = client-server network.
Traps: (1) The slide says five sizes; old past papers say "four". (2) "Expensive, powerful, used for scientific, mathematical and engineering calculations" matches workstation in the slides, but old drive key said supercomputer – read options carefully. (3) Primary storage is temporary, secondary is permanent.

sections.title: Windows and File Management
sections.html:
Desktop

  • Main screen you see after logging on; Windows' main working surface, like the top of a desk.
  • Opened programs/folders show on the taskbar. Parts: desktop icons, Start button, taskbar, notification area.
  • Notification area: far right of taskbar; clock + icons; hover an icon for its info.

Icons and shortcuts

  • Icon: small picture representing a file, folder or program. Open it with a double-click.
  • When Windows first starts, at least one icon appears: the Recycle Bin.
  • Shortcut: icon that is a link to an item, not the item itself. Recognised by the arrow on its icon.
  • Add shortcut: right-click item → Send to → Desktop (create shortcut).
  • Delete an icon: right-click → Delete → Yes. If it is the actual item, the item is deleted; if a shortcut, only the shortcut goes – original stays.
  • Common icons (Computer, Recycle Bin, personal folder): right-click desktop → Personalize → Change desktop icons → tick/untick → OK.
  • Auto arrange: right-click desktop → View → Auto arrange icons. Icons sit on an invisible grid, stacked in columns on the left.
  • Select many icons: click empty area and drag a rectangle around them.
  • Hide/show icons: right-click desktop → View → Show desktop icons (tick toggles).

Recycle Bin

Deleted files go here first, so they can be recovered. Emptying it deletes permanently and frees disk space.

Window parts

Title bar; control buttons Minimize, Maximize, Restore, Close; scroll bars; menu bar; toolbar. Explorer window also: Back/Forward, address bar, search box, navigation pane, file/folder list, details pane.

Files

  • File: resource for storing information, on durable storage; stays available after the program that made it closes. Almost all information in a computer is in a file.
  • Name = name.extension, e.g. lecture2.pptx. Up to 255 characters.
  • Not allowed: \ / : * ? " < > |
  • Extensions: .doc/.docx Word, .ppt/.pptx PowerPoint, .xls/.xlsx Excel, .htm HTML, .exe executable.

File attributes

AttributeMeaning
Read(-only)Can only be read; nothing written
ArchiveTells Windows Backup to back it up
SystemUsed only by the OS; don't alter/delete
HiddenNot shown under normal viewing
DirectoryMarks folders/sub-folders
CompressedReduced size (e.g. .zip)
EncryptedPrevents unauthorised access

View: right-click → Properties → name, location, type, associated program, size, dates created/modified/accessed.

File management

  • Organising files with a file manager (My Computer / Windows Explorer): navigate, basic operations, properties, search.
  • Operations: Create, Copy (same folder → can't have the same name), Move, Delete (to Recycle Bin), Rename (homework1.doc → homeworkFinal.doc).
  • Tips: meaningful names; add revision date/time to names; group related files in one folder; sort by type/name/date; set attributes; always back up.
  • Backup: copies kept in a separate location so they can be restored after disaster/accidental delete.

Folders, file system, paths

  • Folder/directory: container for files and other folders; usually no extension. On a command line called a directory.
  • New folder: right-click → New → Folder (named "New folder"). Rename: right-click → Rename → type → Enter.
  • File system = tree-like; drives get letters (C:, D:); root folder at the top.
  • Absolute path: from the root, e.g. C:\Documents\ICT121\letter1.docx.
  • Relative path: from the current location, e.g. in Documents: ICT121\week1.docx.

Finding files and wildcards

  • Search box on the Start menu (file name, text in file, tags, properties) or in a folder. Options: name, date, type, size.
  • * = 0 or more characters (ICT.* → all files named ICT with any extension).
  • ? = exactly 1 character (????.txt → .txt files with 4-letter names).
  • moswetsi*b.abc matches moswetsi123b.abc; moswetsi?b.abc does not (3 characters, not 1).

sections.title: Internet, WWW and Email
sections.html:
The Internet

  • Worldwide network of networks linking educational, commercial, non-profit, military networks and individuals.
  • Uses the standard TCP/IP protocol suite to link billions of devices.
  • Also called the Net, Information Superhighway, Cyberspace.
  • No one owns it; no single organisation controls it. More a concept than a tangible thing; relies on physical infrastructure. History starts with electronic computers in the 1950s.

Intranet vs extranet

  • Intranet: Internet technology for an organisation's internal use only.
  • Extranet: like an intranet but selected outsiders (e.g. suppliers) can use it.

Internet services: email & discussion groups, research, news, entertainment, downloading, e-shopping, finance, online auctions, careers, e-business, social networking.

World Wide Web

  • System of interlinked hypertext documents accessed via the Internet; runs on servers; multimedia. WWW ≠ Internet (the Web is built on top of the Internet).
  • Hypertext: text with references (hyperlinks) to other text. Hyperlink: a reference you follow by clicking/hovering. HTML: language for creating web documents.
  • Browser: software to retrieve, present and move through web resources; resource identified by a URL. Client-server model: browser = client, web server sends pages back.
  • Slide: two most popular browsers = Microsoft Edge and Mozilla Firefox; others Chrome, Safari, Opera. Browsers also open intranet pages.
  • Mobile browser (microbrowser): stripped-down, fewer features, optimised for small screens and less power/memory.

Web pages, websites, URLs

  • Web page: document usually in HTML, opened with a browser. Website: one or more pages under the same domain name.
  • URL (Uniform Resource Locator) = global address. 3 parts: protocol :// host / location. Protocols: http://, ftp://, mailto://.
  • http://www.google.com: http = protocol; www = World Wide Web (not always needed); google = domain name; .com = domain type.
  • Domains: .com commercial, .org non-profit, .edu education, .net internet-related, .mil US military, .gov US government, .us USA, .uk United Kingdom.
Static pageDynamic page
Delivered exactly as stored; same for everyone; .html; no programming; no web server needed; e.g. a student's profile pageFresh content each view; changes with time/user/interaction; stock prices, weather, online store; client-side script (JavaScript) or server-side (ASP, PHP)

Protocols and security

  • HTTP: viewing web pages; foundation of web data communication. FTP: transferring files between hosts; client-server.
  • HTTPS: HTTP + security, encrypts data (HTTP sends clear text).
  • SSL (Secure Socket Layer): encrypted link between server and client (card numbers, logins). TLS: newer standard, successor to SSL. AES: encryption algorithm for sensitive data.
  • Firewall: blocks unauthorised access to/from a private network; all messages pass through it and those not meeting security criteria are blocked.
  • Search engine: searches the web; results shown on search engine results pages. E.g. Google, Yahoo, MSN, AOL, Ask, AltaVista, Lycos, Dogpile.

Email

  • First email: 1971, Ray Tomlinson, sent to himself.
  • To: main recipients. CC (carbon copy): copied; everyone can see them. BCC (blind carbon copy): hidden from other recipients. Subject: message title.
  • Email window: Send, Attach, Save Draft, Spelling, Cancel; switch HTML ↔ plain text.

sections.title: Introduction to Word Processing
sections.html:
Software recap

  • System software: manages hardware; OS + utilities (maintain/protect, e.g. anti-virus, firewalls).
  • Application software: specific user tasks, e.g. MS Word.

Word processing

  • Using software to create, edit, format, store, retrieve and print text documents. One of the most common PC activities.
  • Examples: Microsoft Word, WordPerfect, AbiWord. Word is part of the Microsoft Office suite and uses a ribbon of tabs with grouped commands.
  • Open Word: Start/Windows button → type "Microsoft Word"; or the apps list; or double-click a desktop shortcut.

Screen elements

ElementWhat it does
File tabBackstage view: open, save, print, share – all file tasks
Quick Access ToolbarOne-click frequent commands; default Save, Undo, Redo
Ribbon / tabs / groupsTask-oriented tabs; group names label related commands; dialog box launcher in group corner
Ribbon Display OptionsAuto-hide Ribbon, Show Tabs, Show Tabs and Commands
AutoSaveSaves every few seconds
Tell meSearch box for commands
Title barFile name + program name; control buttons on the right
Status barFile info left; Read Mode, Print Layout, Web Layout; zoom far right
Share / Comments / Signed-in userSave to cloud and collaborate / comment menu / who is signed in

Saving, closing, opening

  • Formats: .doc (older Word) → .docx successor; .pdf for distributing online; .txt unformatted; .htm/.html web page.
  • Save: first time opens a dialog; after that overwrites the old version. Save As: always opens the dialog – new name or location; the new copy becomes the active document.
  • Close document: small black X or File → Close. Close Word: big red X. Slide says Ctrl+W for closing (in real Word, Ctrl+W closes the document).
  • Open: File → Open → choose file → Open. Up One Level moves up a folder.

Typing and editing keys

KeyEffect
BackspaceDeletes character before the cursor
DeleteDeletes character after
EnterNew line/paragraph
Home / EndStart / end of current line
Pg Up / Pg DnPrevious / next page
Arrows1 character left/right, 1 line up/down
  • Insertion point = cursor.
  • Clipboard: memory area holding cut/copied items. Cut Ctrl+X (removes), Copy Ctrl+C (duplicates), Paste Ctrl+V.
  • Undo recovers from mistakes; Redo reverses an undo. Find/Replace searches and swaps words.
  • Spelling: red wavy line; grammar: green wavy line (Change, Ignore, Add to Dictionary). "Not smart enough" – check yourself.
  • Thesaurus: synonyms and sometimes antonyms.

Formatting

  • Mostly on Home, Insert, Page Layout tabs. Cover page under Insert.
  • Common fonts: Times New Roman, Arial. Size in points; common 10 pt and 12 pt.
  • Slide calls Bold, Italic, Underline, Regular "typefaces" – don't overuse.
  • Lists: bulleted, numbered; increase/decrease level. Indentation: distance of text from the margin.
  • Alignment: left, right, centred, justified (both margins, spacing adjusted).
  • Orientation: default portrait; landscape. Both in one document: section break before and after the pages. Columns.
  • Header top of every page, footer bottom; automatic page numbers.
  • Tables (Insert tab, AutoFit); word wrap moves to next line automatically; paper A4 (US Letter in US).
  • Drawings under Insert: Shapes, ClipArt, WordArt (fancy text). Equation editor under Insert.
  • Template: document that creates a copy of itself when opened (.dotx / .dotm), e.g. business plan; can be protected.

Reviewing

  • Track Changes: click to turn on, edit, click again to turn off.
  • Comment: cursor → New Comment. Delete: right-click → Delete Comment.
  • Accept = document changed; Reject = not updated. Previous/Next to move through changes.

sections.title: Advanced Word Processing II
sections.html:
Tables

  • Insert tab → Table: drag grid, Insert Table, Draw Table, Quick Tables (predesigned). Heading row, cell.
  • Layout tab: insert rows/columns, delete, merge cells, split cells, erase gridlines, cell size, text direction, cell margins, sort, formula, repeat header rows, convert to text.
  • Design tab: table styles gallery (plain, grid, list), shading, borders, border painter.
  • Table alignment = horizontal position between margins; new table aligns left; can centre or right-align. Table move handle drags the table.
  • Convert text → table (choose columns, separator: tabs, commas, paragraphs) and table → text.

Mail merge

  • Sends the same personalised document to many people (e.g. form letter).
  • Combines a main document (wording same for everyone) with a data source (variable list).
  • Field = one item of information (column), e.g. Last name. Record = all fields for one person = a row. Header row has field names.
  • Data sources: Word document, Access table/query, Excel worksheet, Outlook contacts.
  • Mailings tab: Start Mail Merge → Select Recipients (type new list / use existing / Outlook) → Edit Recipient List (sort, filter, find duplicates) → insert merge fields (Address Block, Greeting Line) → Preview → Finish & Merge.

Electronic forms

Structured document completed electronically; Developer tab, Design Mode, content controls.

ControlUse
Rich TextLots of formatted text, can include images and tables
Plain TextText/numbers readable by any editor; limited formatting
PictureInsert a picture
Building Block GalleryReusable content, e.g. header, disclaimer
Check BoxSelect/deselect an item
Combo BoxList and you can type your own entry
Drop-Down ListChoose from fixed list only
Date PickerPick from calendar
Repeating SectionRepeats content within one control

Academic documents (References tab)

  • Table of Contents: generated automatically; page numbers update as document grows/shrinks.
  • Table of Figures: lists figures, pictures, tables (from captions) like a ToC.
  • Style manual: rules for margins, spacing, footnotes/endnotes, citations, bibliography. Plagiarising = passing off another's ideas/words.
  • Styles: MLA humanities; APA business, economics, communication, social sciences; Chicago papers and books; Turabian history papers.
  • Citation: Insert Citation → Add New Source. Manage Sources (master list = all documents; current list = this document). Bibliography button inserts list.
  • Footnotes: bottom of the page, numbered 1, 2, 3. Endnotes: end of document, numbered i, ii, iii. Both superscript; used for references and explanations. Delete: select the number in the text → Delete.

sections.title: Hardware
sections.html:
Key concepts

  • Computer system: hardware + software working together to convert data into information.
  • Hardware: input devices, memory, CPU, output devices, storage devices.
  • Input devices enter data/instructions; CPU controls main functions; memory = temporary; storage = permanent; output = human-readable results.

System unit and motherboard

  • System unit: case holding the electronic components. PC (tower/desktop, separate monitor), laptop (clamshell), tablet (touch screen), smartphone (handheld).
  • Motherboard: all components attach to it; keyboard/mouse connect directly; others use expansion slots and ports.
  • Inside: power supply, chip, fan, video card, modem card, sound card, hard drive, CD/DVD drive, ribbon cable.

Data representation

  • Binary: only 0 and 1 (off/on).
  • Bit = binary digit (smallest unit). Byte = 8 bits = one character. Nibble = 4 bits.
  • KB ≈ 1000 bytes (exactly 1024); MB = 1024 KB (~1 million characters); GB = 1024 MB (~1 billion); TB = 1024 GB; PB = 1024 TB; EB = 1024 PB.

CPU

  • "Brain"; follows software instructions. Control unit + ALU, both with registers (high-speed storage). Linked by the bus.
  • System clock sets speed. Old: MHz (million cycles/s); now GHz (billion cycles/s). Faster = more power and heat.
  • Multicore: 2+ cores on one chip → multiple tasks at once, better performance, less power.
  • Control unit: stores instruction set, fetches and interprets instructions, passes maths/logic to ALU, directs data flow, coordinates.
  • ALU: "calculator"; arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷) and logical (comparisons =, >, <, ≥, ≤, ≠).
  • Machine cycle: Fetch → Decode → Execute → Store.

Input devices

  • OCR: software recognising individual characters. OMR: detects simple marks (e.g. multiple-choice sheets).
  • Bar code reader: measures reflected light from bar code. Touch screen: pressure-sensitive covering. Voice recognition: spoken commands via microphone + sound card.
  • Others: keyboard, mouse, game pad, joystick, scanner, webcam, microphone, magnetic strip reader, iris/fingerprint/signature scanner.

Storage

PrimarySecondary
Temporary; directly accessed by CPU; fast; more expensivePermanent; large; non-volatile; cheap; slower
  • Volatile: lost when power off (RAM). Non-volatile: kept (ROM – fixed contents).
  • Choosing storage: capacity and speed. Storage medium = physical material holding data.
  • Optical disks use lasers. CD-ROM prerecorded; CD-R write once; CD-RW rewrite many times. DVD holds more: 4.7 GB single, 9.4 GB double-sided (slide). DVD-R once; DVD-RW/DVD-RAM/DVD+RW reusable. Blu-ray: HD video, large data.
  • Flash drive: portable, USB, re-writable. Magnetic tape: mass storage, backup.
  • Cloud storage: back up over the internet to a vendor's server: Dropbox, iCloud, Google Drive, OneDrive, IDrive, Mega, Box, pCloud.

Output devices

Visual display units: CRT (cathode ray tube) vs LCD (liquid crystal display). Printers: dot-matrix, inkjet, laser. Speakers.

o: Directly accessible by the CPU at register speed

sections.title: Software
sections.html:
The slide file calls itself "Lecture 5 – Software".

Two types

  • Application software: solves a particular user problem / entertainment.
  • System software: runs at the most basic level; lets applications use the hardware; manages resources. Examples: OS, utility programs, device drivers, program translators.

Operating system

  • Principal system software; low-level master programs managing basic operations. Every general-purpose computer needs one. Apps are written for a particular OS.
  • Functions: booting, CPU management, file management, task management, security management; plus resource allocation (processes, storage, memory, devices) and controlling program execution.
  • Booting = loading the OS into main memory. 4 steps: (1) power on (2) diagnostic tests of memory/CPU/hardware (3) BIOS copied to main memory (4) boot program loads the OS.
  • Bootstrap program: stored in ROM, runs at start-up, loads the kernel. Kernel/supervisor: always running, stays in memory, manages the CPU.
  • Memory management: stops programs overlapping, swaps parts in and out, tracks virtual memory.
  • File management: data file vs program file; hierarchical directories; pathname e.g. C:/MyDocuments/Termpaper/section1.doc.
  • Task management: multitasking = more than one program at once (word processing + music); OS alternates processor time.
  • Security management: ID + password.

Types of OS

TypeMeaningExamples
Single-user single-taskingOne user, one taskMS-DOS, Palm OS
Single-user multitaskingOne user, several tasks; common in PCsWindows, Linux, Mac OS X
Multi-user multitaskingMany users at once; mainframes/supercomputersUNIX, Linux, VMS
Multi-processing2+ CPUsLinux, Unix, Windows 2000/XP, Mac OS X
Network OSPCs share resourcesWindows 2008 Server, NetWare
Real-time OSBuilt into devices, quick response: ATMs, flight control, medical devicesSymbian, PalmOS, Windows CE

User interfaces

  • GUI: mouse/keys select icons and menus. Three main features: desktop, icons, menus. Rollover = text box explaining an icon on hover. Menus: pull-down, cascading, pull-up, pop-up.
  • Command-line interface: type commands; user must know them.

Other system software

  • Device drivers: let input/output devices talk to the computer; come with OS, with the hardware, or download from the maker.
  • Utilities: configure, analyse, optimise, maintain: file manager, uninstaller, antivirus, compression, pop-up blocker, backup, firewall.
  • Program translators: convert source code (C++, Java – human-readable) to machine code.

Application software

TypeExamples
Document productionMS Word, WordPerfect, FrontPage, OpenOffice Writer
Numerical analysisMS Excel, Lotus 1-2-3, SPSS
PresentationPowerPoint, OpenOffice Impress, Corel Presentations
DatabasesMS Access, Oracle, DB2
GraphicsPaint, CorelDraw, AutoCAD
  • Generic / off-the-shelf / packaged: ready-made, general purpose (word processors).
  • Custom / tailor-made / bespoke: made for one company, e.g. BTC billing system, UB student management system.
  • Open source: free, anyone can modify and distribute: Moodle, Linux, FrontlineSMS, WordPress.
  • Web application: runs on a remote server through a browser: Dropbox, Google Docs.
  • In-house: built by the company's own IT department. Proprietary: licensed, exclusive rights of owner. Rentalware: leased online for a fee.
  • Freeware: free to use, can't sell it, developer keeps copyright (some anti-virus). Shareware: free trial, then pay/register.
  • Software suites (integrated packages): MS Office 2010, Corel WordPerfect Office X7, Apache OpenOffice.

sections.title: Information Networks
sections.html:
Telecommunications and networks

  • Telecommunications: electronic transmission of signals (telephone, radio, TV); reduces barriers of time and distance.
  • Network: media, devices and software connecting 2+ computers/devices to communicate and share. Devices on it = nodes.
AdvantagesDisadvantages
Share peripherals (printers, scanners), software, data; better communication; database access; centralised admin and support; easy maintenance; security via better backupsCost; security risks; dependency on infrastructure; complexity/expertise; bandwidth limits and congestion; privacy; downtime; compatibility; scalability
  • Synchronous: received almost instantly – phone call, instant messaging (MSN). Asynchronous: delay of hours/days – post, email.
  • Telecom model: sender → telecom device → medium → telecom device → receiver (reversible).

Network components

  • Send/receive devices (computers; any attached device = node). Communication devices: NIC, modem, servers.
  • Server controls the client/server network; manages files and printers.
  • Transmission media = most important component. Wired/guided: twisted pair, coaxial, fibre-optic, broadband over power lines. Wireless: microwave (terrestrial, satellite), 3G/4G, Wi-Fi, NFC, Bluetooth, ultra wideband, infrared.
  • NOS (network OS): controls devices on a network, like an OS for the network. Protocol: rules for exchanging information over a channel.

Network types

TypeAreaExample
PANOne person's devicesPhone + earbuds
LANBuilding/campusUB Gaborone campus
MANLANs in one cityFNB branches in Gaborone
WANCities/continents; complex equipment; many mediaBanks' ATMs; largest WAN = the Internet

Topologies

  • Bus: all nodes on one main linear cable with a terminator at each end.
  • Star: nodes connect through a central device/server.
  • Ring: each node linked to the two nearest → circle.

Architecture

  • Client/server: clients request, servers supply. File server (shared disk), print server (schedules print jobs), mail server.
  • Peer-to-peer (P2P): all computers equal, communicate directly, no server.

Remote access and connecting

  • Telnet (remote logon): log on to other computers, e.g. library holdings. FTP: transfer files. SSH: UNIX-based secure remote access. File sharing: Google Drive, Dropbox.
  • Dial-up: temporary, analog phone lines; needs phone line, ISP, modem (MOdulator/DEModulator); 56 Kbps.
  • Dedicated line: fixed bandwidth, reserved 24/7, e.g. ADSL (Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line) 128 Kbps – 8.45 Mbps. Bandwidth = data transmission rate.

sections.title: Health, Security and Legal Issues
sections.html:
The slide file calls itself "Lecture 10".

Health

  • RSI (Repetitive Strain Injury): pain in muscles, nerves, tendons from repetitive movement and overuse; from long typing/mouse use and switching between them; worse under stress, deadlines, bad keyboard placement.
  • Tendonitis: inflamed tendon; pain forearm to hand, tingling fingers. Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: inflamed nerve forearm → palm of wrist; burning pain, numb/tingling fingers.
  • Prevent RSI: correct typing technique and posture, right equipment, good habits, breaks, shake dangling arms, keyboard/mouse not near desk edge, wrists not resting or bent while typing.
  • Monitor radiation: old screens linked to cancer, miscarriage, birth defects; new standards cut exposure; FDA tested hundreds, rarely unsafe.
  • Computer Vision Syndrome (CVS): eye strain/irritation. Causes: bad lighting, distance, glare, posture. Prevent: breaks, monitor at a distance, straight in front, adjust lighting / anti-glare filter.
  • Ergonomics: applied science of comfort, efficiency, safety in workplace design: posture, positioning, copy holders, adjustable chair/desk. Picture: top of monitor at eye level, ~20 inches away, feet flat, knees level/lower than hips, working surface at elbow height, back supported.

Safety-critical systems

  • Failure → loss of life, major property or environmental damage: railway/road control, nuclear power stations, medical databases. Need rigorous development and reliability testing.
  • Fault: flaw (wrong instruction). Failure: unexpected behaviour caused by a fault (wrong drug dose). Hazard: event/state that can lead to an accident. Mishap/accident: unplanned event that may injure/kill.

Security

  • Protecting hardware, software and information from theft, damage, disruption. Physical vs logical/electronic.
  • CIA: Confidentiality (private), Integrity (complete, unaltered, changed only by authorised people), Availability (there when needed – prevent DoS).
  • Physical risks: water drainage, air conditioning, fire-proof materials, UPS, regular backups.
  • Hacking: exploiting security flaws to get information without the owner's knowledge. Professional hackers (profit, corporate espionage); hobbyists (fun, learning); internal users (disgruntled employees); crackers (break security, "hardcore"); hacktivists (political activism).
  • Virus: attaches to files, needs humans to spread. Worm: spreads itself. Trojan horse: hidden in safe-looking software (steal card numbers, DoS).
  • Password attack (weak passwords); communication intercept (secretly reads/alters messages); Denial of Service (floods system so legit users can't use it).
  • Defences: firewalls (logs detect attacks), strong password policy, anti-virus (keep definitions up to date), encryption, education, backups.

Legal

  • Problems: plagiarism, software piracy, copyright infringement.
  • Plagiarism: unauthorised/uncited use of someone's intellectual property (ownership of original works/inventions). Copyright infringement = plagiarism of copyrighted material.
  • Protection: Patent (secures an invention for a time), Copyright (exclusive right to produce, reproduce, publish, perform a work), User licence (licensor grants licensee privileges, e.g. copying software).
  • Freeware: no cost to copy – Adobe Reader, Avast Free. Shareware: copyrighted, use without licence for a trial, then pay – WinZip, Adobe Photoshop. Commercial: must be bought, not copied; organisations use a site licence.

sections.title: Practical book (Moodle) – Windows and Word skills
sections.html:
These topics are in the Moodle practical book (Using the computer; Moodle/Outlook/Teams; Desktop; File Explorer; Word chapters 6–10), not in the lecture slides. Filled from standard Windows and Word knowledge – not in your slides.

Keyboard, mouse, start and shut down

  • Start: press power button → boot → log in. Shut down: Start → Power → Shut down (don't just pull the plug). Restart, Sleep also there.
  • Keys: Shift (capitals/symbols), Caps Lock, Tab, Esc (cancel), Ctrl/Alt (shortcuts), Windows key (Start menu), function keys F1–F12 (F1 = Help), numeric keypad (Num Lock).
  • Mouse: click (select), double-click (open), right-click (shortcut/context menu), drag (move), scroll wheel.
  • Scroll bars: vertical (up/down) and horizontal (left/right); drag the scroll box or click arrows.

Desktop, taskbar, windows

  • Taskbar: Start button, search box, pinned/open program buttons, notification area.
  • Switch windows: click its taskbar button, or Alt + Tab. Launch apps from Start, search, or shortcut.
  • Minimize (hide to taskbar), Maximize (fill screen), Restore Down, Close. Resize by dragging a border/corner; move by dragging the title bar.
  • Dialog box: small window asking for options/confirmation (OK, Cancel, tabs, check boxes, option buttons).
  • Menus: click the name, choose a command; … after a command opens a dialog box; ▸ opens a sub-menu; greyed = unavailable.

File Explorer

  • Open: Windows key + E, folder icon on taskbar, or Start.
  • Parts: ribbon (Home, Share, View), address bar, navigation pane (left), Quick access (pinned/frequent folders), file list, search box, status bar, preview/details pane.
  • New folder: Ctrl + Shift + N or Home → New folder. Rename: F2. Delete: Delete key. Permanently delete: Shift + Delete. Select all: Ctrl + A.
  • Search box searches the current folder. Customise via View tab: icons, list, details; show file name extensions, hidden items.

Moodle, Outlook, Teams

  • Moodle: open-source course management system (log in and out with student ID and password).
  • Outlook: Office 365 email; Teams: chat, meetings, classes; both through Office 365 login.

Word skills

  • Select: drag; double-click = word, triple-click = paragraph, Ctrl + A = all; Shift + arrows.
  • Shortcuts: Ctrl+B bold, Ctrl+I italic, Ctrl+U underline, Ctrl+S save, F12 = Save As, Ctrl+O open, Ctrl+N new, Ctrl+P print, Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+Y redo, Ctrl+F find, Ctrl+H replace, Ctrl+E centre, Ctrl+J justify, Ctrl+L left, Ctrl+R right, F7 spelling & grammar, Shift+F7 thesaurus, Ctrl+Home / Ctrl+End start/end of document, Ctrl+Enter page break.
  • Superscript (x² – Ctrl+Shift+=) and subscript (H₂O – Ctrl+=).
  • Line spacing: Home → Paragraph (1.0, 1.15, 1.5, 2.0). Margins, orientation, size: Layout tab. Page numbers, header, footer: Insert tab.
  • Borders and shading; WordArt and shapes on Insert. Templates: File → New → choose; save your own as .dotx. Forms: Developer tab content controls.
  • Print: File → Print (Ctrl+P): choose printer, copies, page range. Exit Word: File → Close / X.

sets.title: Word processing test
sets.desc: 228 questions covering every slide of Lectures 4 and 5.

qs.q: Which category of software is used for managing and controlling hardware components and allows interaction between the hardware and software?
qs.x: System software manages the hardware and lets hardware and software interact. Examples: the operating system and utility software.

qs.q: Anti-virus software and firewalls are examples of:
qs.x: Utility software helps maintain and protect the computer system. It falls under system software.

qs.q: Microsoft Word is an example of:
qs.x: Application software is designed for specific end-user tasks, e.g. MS Word.

qs.q: Which ONE of the following is NOT system software?
qs.x: Word is application software. The OS and utility programs (anti-virus, firewalls) are system software.

qs.q: Utility software is best described as software that:
o: Helps maintain and protect the computer system
Performs specific end-user tasks such as typing letters
Combines a main document with a data source
qs.x: The lecture defines utility software as software that helps maintain and protect the computer system.

qs.q: Word processing involves using suitable software to do all of the following EXCEPT:
qs.x: Word processing = create, edit, format, store, retrieve and print text documents. Managing hardware is the job of system software.

qs.q: A word processor is:
o: Electronic application software that performs composition, editing, formatting and sometimes printing of documents
System software that controls the printer and other hardware
Utility software that protects documents from viruses
A hardware device used to type documents
qs.x: That is the lecture's definition of a word processor.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a word processor?
qs.x: The examples of word processors given are Microsoft Word, WordPerfect and AbiWord. Excel is a spreadsheet program.

qs.q: Which of the following documents would you normally create with a word processor?
qs.x: Examples of word-processed documents: letters, CVs, reports, books, newsletters.

qs.q: Microsoft Word is part of the:
qs.x: Word is part of the Microsoft Office Suite.

qs.q: In Microsoft Word, tabs containing groups of related commands make up the:
qs.x: Word features ribbons: tabs with commands, where related commands are grouped together (e.g. File, Home, Page Layout tabs).

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a way of opening MS Word given in the lecture?
o: Clicking the Windows button and searching for "Microsoft Word"
Scrolling through the list of installed applications
Double-clicking a Word shortcut icon on the desktop
qs.x: Ctrl + W is the close shortcut. The three ways to open Word: search, scroll the app list, or double-click a desktop shortcut.

qs.q: The Windows button is usually located at the:
o: Bottom left corner of the screen
Top right corner of the screen
Top left corner of the screen
Bottom right corner of the screen
qs.x: The lecture says the Windows button is usually located in the bottom left corner of your screen.

qs.q: Clicking the File tab displays the Microsoft Office ______ view.
qs.x: The File tab displays Backstage view, a centralized space for file management tasks.

qs.q: Backstage view is a centralized space for:
o: File management tasks such as opening, saving, printing, publishing or sharing a file
qs.x: Backstage view = all the things you can do WITH a file.

qs.q: The default commands on the Quick Access Toolbar are:
qs.x: The Quick Access Toolbar displays frequently used commands; the defaults are Save, Undo and Redo.

qs.q: Which screen element saves your document every few seconds so you don't have to?
qs.x: AutoSave saves the document every few seconds.

qs.q: The three ways you can display the ribbon using Ribbon Display Options are:
o: Auto-hide Ribbon, Show Tabs, Show Tabs and Commands
Read Mode, Print Layout, Web Layout
qs.x: Ribbon Display Options: Auto-hide Ribbon, Show Tabs, or Show Tabs and Commands.

qs.q: The window control buttons are:
o: Read Mode, Print Layout and Web Layout
qs.x: Window control buttons display commands to Minimize, Restore Down or Close the window.

qs.q: The title bar displays:
o: The name of the file and the name of the program
The page number and word count
qs.x: The title bar shows the file name and program name; window control buttons sit on its right side.

qs.q: On the status bar, which information is shown on the LEFT side?
o: File information such as page number and word count
Read Mode, Print Layout and Web Layout buttons
qs.x: Status bar: file information on the left; view buttons on the right; zoom controls at the far right edge.

qs.q: Read Mode, Print Layout and Web Layout buttons are found on the:
qs.x: The right side of the status bar holds the Read Mode, Print Layout and Web Layout view buttons.

qs.q: Zoom controls are located:
o: On the far right edge of the status bar
On the title bar next to the file name
qs.x: The far right edge of the status bar displays the Zoom controls.

qs.q: The "Tell me what you want to do" box:
o: Searches for Office commands, refining the results with every keystroke
Displays the name of the signed-in user
Saves the document to the cloud
qs.x: It is a search feature for commands; every keystroke refines the results so you can click the command as soon as it displays.

qs.q: Which screen element lets you save your file to the cloud and collaborate, or email the file or a PDF of it through Outlook?
qs.x: The Share button opens the Share dialog box for cloud saving, collaboration and emailing.

qs.q: Group names on the ribbon:
o: Indicate the name of the groups of related commands on the displayed tab
Show the name of the file and program
List the names of the task-oriented tabs
Show which user is signed in
qs.x: Group names (e.g. Clipboard, Font, Paragraph, Styles, Editing) name the groups of related commands.

qs.q: Ribbon tabs:
o: Display the names of the task-oriented tabs relevant to the open document
Display commands to Minimize, Restore Down or Close
Display file information and zoom controls
Display a short menu for adding comments
qs.x: Ribbon tabs = the names of the task-oriented tabs (Home, Insert, Design, Layout, etc.).

qs.q: The small arrow in the bottom-right corner of a ribbon group, which opens a dialog box with more options, is the:
qs.x: The Ribbon slide labels this arrow the Dialog box launcher.

qs.q: The ribbon displays a group of task-oriented tabs that contain:
o: The commands, styles and resources you need to work in Office desktop apps
Only the Save, Undo and Redo commands
The file name and program name
qs.x: That is the lecture's definition of the ribbon.

qs.q: The signed-in user element:
o: Identifies the user who is signed in to Office
Shows the author of every comment
Lists people the file is shared with
qs.x: Signed-in user identifies the user who is signed in to Office (signing in is optional).

qs.q: Clicking the Comments button:
o: Displays a short menu to add a comment or view existing comments
qs.x: Comments displays a short menu from which you can add a comment or view comments already in the document.

qs.q: On Word's start (Home) screen, recently opened documents display under:
qs.x: The start screen shows Recent, Pinned and Shared with Me; recently opened documents display under Recent.

qs.q: On Word's start screen, Account, Feedback and Options let you:
o: View account information, give feedback to Microsoft and open the Word Options dialog box
Change the page orientation and margins
qs.x: These sit at the bottom left of the start screen.

qs.q: On Word's start screen, which option do you click to start a new empty document?
qs.x: "Start a blank document here" points at Blank document. New lets you search for templates.

qs.q: Saving your work to a file ensures that the text, graphics and other elements in your document are:
qs.x: Saving writes the document's contents to a disk.

qs.q: Which file format is the successor of the .doc format?
qs.x: .DOC is the format used by Word, while .DOCX is its successor.

qs.q: Which file format is widely used for distributing documents over the Internet?
qs.x: .pdf is widely used for distributing documents over the Internet.

qs.q: To save a document as an UNFORMATTED text file, you save it as:
qs.x: .txt saves a document as an unformatted text file.

qs.q: To save a Word document as a Web page, you use the format:
qs.x: .htm or .html saves a Word document as a Web page.

qs.q: When you use Save on a NEW document for the first time, Word:
o: Displays a dialog box where you choose where to save it and give it a name
Saves it automatically with no questions
Writes it over an older version
qs.x: First save → Word displays a dialog box to choose location and name.

qs.q: When you click Save on an EXISTING document you have been editing:
o: The newly saved version is written over the older version
A copy is saved under a different name
qs.x: Saving an existing document overwrites the older version.

qs.q: Which command ALWAYS displays a dialog box where you can choose a document name and disk?
qs.x: Save As always displays the dialog box. Save only does so the first time.

qs.q: You want to keep your original report and save an edited copy in a different folder under a new name. You should use:
qs.x: Use Save As to save a copy under a different name or in a different folder (or disk).

qs.q: After using Save As, which document is open on your screen?
o: The newly saved copy becomes the active document
The original document stays the active document
Both documents open side by side
No document; Word closes the file
qs.x: The newly saved copy becomes the active document.

qs.q: In the Save As dialog box, the box where you choose the file format (e.g. Word Document *.docx) is:
qs.x: Save as type sets the format; File name sets the name.

qs.q: To close a DOCUMENT (not Word itself), you click:
o: The close box with the small (black) X, or Close from the File menu
The close box with the large red X only
qs.x: Small black X or File → Close closes the document.

qs.q: According to the lecture, the keyboard shortcut for closing the Word application is:
qs.x: The slide gives Ctrl + W, so answer that in the test. (In real Word, Ctrl + W closes the document and Alt + F4 closes the program.)

qs.q: To close the Word APPLICATION, you click:
o: The close box with the large (red) X on the title bar
The close box with the small (black) X
qs.x: The large red X closes the Word application.

qs.q: To open an existing file, you:
o: Select Open from the File menu, click the file name, then click the Open button
Click Save As and choose the file
qs.x: File → Open → click the file name → Open.

qs.q: In the Open dialog box, if your file is not in the opened folder, you click:
o: The down arrow next to the folder name to see a directory listing
qs.x: The down arrow next to the folder name shows a directory listing.

qs.q: The Up One Level button in the Open dialog box:
o: Moves you up one folder level
Opens the file one level deeper
Moves the cursor up one line
qs.x: Up One Level enables you to move up one level, then switch to where the file is.

qs.q: The text insertion point in Word is also called the:
qs.x: Text insertion point = cursor.

qs.q: Which key inserts a NewLine character?
qs.x: Enter: NewLine character.

qs.q: Which key deletes the PREVIOUS character (the one before the cursor)?
qs.x: Backspace deletes the previous character; Delete deletes the next character.

qs.q: Which key deletes the NEXT character (the one after the cursor)?
qs.x: Delete: delete next character.

qs.q: The Spacebar inserts a:
qs.x: Spacebar: space character.

qs.q: Pressing the Home key moves the insertion point to the:
qs.x: Home → beginning of current line.

qs.q: Pressing the End key moves the insertion point to the:
qs.x: End → end of current line.

qs.q: Which key moves the insertion point to the NEXT page?
qs.x: Pg Dn moves to the next page; Pg Up moves to the previous page.

qs.q: Pg Up moves the insertion point:
o: To the beginning of the line
qs.x: Pg Up → previous page.

qs.q: The Down arrow key moves the insertion point:
o: To the end of the document
qs.x: Down arrow → 1 line down; Up arrow → 1 line up.

qs.q: The Right arrow key moves the insertion point:
o: To the end of the line
qs.x: The slide has a typo (it says the right arrow moves left). The right arrow really moves one character to the right.

qs.q: The Office Clipboard is:
o: An area of memory reserved to temporarily hold selections that have been cut or copied
A toolbar with Save, Undo and Redo
A folder on the disk where documents are saved
A tab on the ribbon for formatting text
qs.x: That is the lecture's definition of the Office Clipboard.

qs.q: Cut:
o: Removes a selection from its original location and places it in the Office Clipboard
Duplicates a selection and leaves the original in place
Places a copied selection into another location
Deletes text permanently without using the Clipboard
qs.x: Cut removes the selection (Ctrl + X); Copy duplicates it (Ctrl + C).

qs.q: The keyboard shortcut for Copy is:
qs.x: Ctrl + C = Copy, Ctrl + X = Cut, Ctrl + V = Paste.

qs.q: The keyboard shortcut for Paste is:
qs.x: Paste places a cut or copied selection into another location: Ctrl + V.

qs.q: The keyboard shortcut for Cut is:
qs.x: Ctrl + X = Cut.

qs.q: What is the main difference between Cut and Copy?
o: Cut removes the selection from its original location; Copy leaves the original in place
Copy removes the selection; Cut leaves the original in place
Cut uses the Clipboard but Copy does not
qs.x: Both put the selection on the Clipboard; only Cut removes the original.

qs.q: Cut, Copy, Paste and Format Painter are found in which group on the Home tab?
qs.x: The Relocating Text slide shows them in the Clipboard group.

qs.q: Undo:
qs.x: Undo enables recovery from mistakes; Redo is for reversing undo.

qs.q: Redo is used for:
qs.x: Redo: for reversing undo.

qs.q: The Undo and Redo buttons are located on the:
qs.x: The Undo/Redo slide shows them on the Quick Access Toolbar, above the File and Home tabs.

qs.q: Which feature is used for searching for specific words and even replacing them with new words?
qs.x: Find/Replace, in the Editing group.

qs.q: The Find and Replace dialog box has which three tabs?
qs.x: Find, Replace, Go To.

qs.q: Find, Replace and Select are found in which group?
qs.x: They are in the Editing group on the Home tab.

qs.q: When the spell checker flags a word, which three choices does the lecture list?
o: Change, Ignore or Add To Dictionary
qs.x: Spell/grammar checking: Change, Ignore or Add To Dictionary.

qs.q: How does MS Word flag a possible GRAMMAR error?
qs.x: Grammar: green wavy line. Spelling: red wavy line.

qs.q: How does MS Word flag a possible SPELLING error?
qs.x: Automatic spell checking uses a red wavy line.

qs.q: The lecture gives a WARNING about the spell and grammar checker. What is it?
o: Be careful, it is not smart enough
It only works in Read Mode
qs.x: "Be careful → Not smart enough!" Always proofread yourself.

qs.q: The thesaurus displays:
qs.x: Thesaurus: for displaying synonyms & sometimes antonyms.

qs.q: In the lecture's thesaurus example for the word "after", which word is the ANTONYM?
qs.x: after: afterwards, next, later (synonyms), before (antonym).

qs.q: Formatting features allow us to:
qs.x: Formatting allows us to change document appearance.

qs.q: Most formatting tools in MS Word are found under the:
o: Home, Insert and Page Layout tabs
qs.x: The lecture: mostly under Home, Insert & Page Layout.

qs.q: A cover page is found under the ______ tab.
qs.x: Cover page: under the Insert tab.

qs.q: The purpose of a cover page is to:
o: Introduce the document and give it a professional finish
List the sources cited in the document
Show the page numbers of headings
Hold notes at the end of each page
qs.x: A cover page introduces the document and gives it a professional finish. Many templates are available.

qs.q: According to the lecture, the most commonly used font types are:
qs.x: Most commonly used: Times New Roman & Arial.

qs.q: Font size (text size) is measured in:
qs.x: Text size is in points, e.g. 28 pt, 40 pt.

qs.q: The most commonly used font sizes are:
qs.x: Most commonly used sizes: 10pt and 12pt. (28 pt and 40 pt are just examples of sizes.)

qs.q: According to the lecture, which of the following is NOT a typeface?
qs.x: The lecture lists typefaces as Bold, Italics, Underlined and regular. Calibri is a font type.

qs.q: What advice does the lecture give about bold, italics and underline?
o: Use them on every heading and paragraph
Use them instead of changing font size
qs.x: Typefaces highlight certain parts of text. Do not overuse.

qs.q: Indentation determines:
o: How part of a paragraph is distanced from the margin
The position of the table between margins
The number of columns on a page
qs.x: Indentation = how part of a paragraph is distanced from the margin (Decrease level / Increase level buttons).

qs.q: The two types of lists shown in the lecture are:
qs.x: Bulleted list (• ICT121) and numbered list (i. ICT121).

qs.q: Which alignment makes all lines start at the same horizontal distance from the left margin?
qs.x: Left justified: all lines start at the same horizontal distance from the left margin.

qs.q: Text that starts at the left margin and ends at the right margin, with the spaces adjusted to make this happen, is:
qs.x: Justified: starts at the left margin and ends at the right margin; spaces adjusted.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four text alignments shown in the lecture?
qs.x: The four alignments: left, centre, right, justified.

qs.q: By default, new documents are displayed in:
qs.x: By default, new documents are in portrait.

qs.q: You want ONE page of a portrait report to be in landscape. What must you do?
o: Insert a section break before and another after the affected page, then apply landscape
Change the whole document to landscape
Insert a page break, then press Ctrl + L
Insert a footer on that page
qs.x: How: insert a section break before and another after the affected page(s), then apply the preferred orientation.

qs.q: Page orientation (Portrait/Landscape) is found on the ______ tab.
qs.x: Orientation, Size and Columns are on the Page Layout tab.

qs.q: Which feature lets text flow in two or more vertical sections across a page, like a newspaper?
qs.x: Columns: you can have multiple columns.

qs.q: A header is placed at the:
qs.x: Header: top of every page. Footer: bottom of every page.

qs.q: A footer is placed at the:
qs.x: Footer: at the bottom of every page.

qs.q: Why should you let MS Word insert page numbers automatically?
o: To ensure pages have the correct page numbers
To create a table of figures
qs.x: MS Word can automatically insert page numbers to ensure pages have correct page numbers.

qs.q: Tables are inserted from the ______ tab.
qs.x: Tables: under Insert tab.

qs.q: Instead of setting the height and width of table columns yourself, you can use:
qs.x: Set/change height/width or use AutoFit.

qs.q: Wrap-around (word wrap) means that MS Word:
o: Automatically moves to the next line when a line of text is filled
Wraps text around a picture only
Moves text to the next page when you press Enter
Wraps the document in a cover page
qs.x: Word wrap moves to the next line automatically; text readjusts when margins change.

qs.q: The usual paper size is:
qs.x: Paper size: usually A4 (in the US it is US Letter).

qs.q: In the United States, the usual paper size is:
qs.x: Usually A4, but US Letter in the US.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the drawing options under the Insert tab listed in the lecture?
qs.x: Drawings: Shapes, ClipArt and WordArt (fancy text). Track Changes is on the Review tab.

qs.q: WordArt is described in the lecture as:
qs.x: WordArt (fancy text).

qs.q: The Equation Editor is found under the ______ tab and is used for typing equations such as the quadratic formula.
qs.x: Equation Editor: for equations, under the Insert tab (Symbols group).

qs.q: A document that creates a copy of itself when opened is a:
qs.x: Template: a document that creates a copy of itself when opened.

qs.q: Word templates are saved with which file extensions?
qs.x: Templates: .dotx or .dotm.

qs.q: A business plan with a predefined page layout, fonts, margins and styles is an example of a:
qs.x: The lecture's template example is a business plan with predefined layout, fonts, margins and styles.

qs.q: Which part of a template can be protected, according to the lecture?
qs.x: Template can be protected e.g. a disclaimer.

qs.q: Track Changes is used for:
o: Tracking changes when reviewing a document
Searching for words and replacing them
Saving a copy under a different name
qs.x: Track Changes: for tracking changes when reviewing a document.

qs.q: Track Changes is found on the ______ tab.
qs.x: Review tab, Tracking group.

qs.q: How do you activate Track Changes?
o: Click Track Changes on the Review tab
Right-click the text and choose Track
qs.x: To activate: click Track Changes.

qs.q: How do you deactivate Track Changes?
qs.x: To deactivate: click Track Changes again.

qs.q: With Track Changes on, which of these edits are tracked?
o: Deleting, inserting, moving and formatting text
qs.x: Make changes: delete, insert, move, format, etc.

qs.q: To add a comment, you:
o: Place the cursor where you want the comment and click New Comment
qs.x: Place cursor → click New Comment.

qs.q: To delete a comment, you:
o: Right-click the comment, then select Delete Comment
qs.x: Right-click on the comment, then select Delete Comment.

qs.q: When you ACCEPT a change:
o: The document is modified to reflect the new change
The change is turned into a comment
qs.x: Accept: document is modified to reflect new changes.

qs.q: When you REJECT a change:
o: The document is modified to include the change
The change is saved as a new version
qs.x: Reject: document not updated.

qs.q: The Previous and Next buttons in the Changes group are for:
o: Moving to the previous and next page
qs.x: Previous/Next: for navigating through suggested changes.

qs.q: The Comments group on the Review tab contains:
o: New Comment, Delete, Previous and Next
Track Changes, Show Markup and Reviewing Pane
qs.x: Comments group: New Comment, Delete, Previous, Next.

qs.q: In the markup view shown in the lecture, where do comments and deleted text appear?
o: In balloons in the right margin
At the bottom of every page
qs.x: The More on Comments slide shows balloons such as "Comment [RSS1]" and "Deleted: …" in the right margin.

qs.q: In a Word table, the box where a row and a column meet is called a:
qs.x: The Table Introduction slide labels it a cell.

qs.q: The top row of a table that holds the column titles is the:
qs.x: The Budget Analysis example labels it the heading row.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT an option on the Insert → Table menu?
qs.x: Options: drag the grid, Insert Table, Draw Table, Convert Text to Table, Excel Spreadsheet, Quick Tables.

qs.q: Quick Tables lets you:
qs.x: Quick Tables → insert a predesigned table.

qs.q: Which table option lets you create a table by drawing its borders yourself?
qs.x: Draw Table → draw a table.

qs.q: In the lecture's screenshot, the Merge Cells button is dimmed because:
o: The cells to merge are not selected
The table has no heading row
qs.x: Merge Cells is dimmed because cells to merge are not selected.

qs.q: "Company Expenditures" stretches across the whole top of the table in the lecture example. Which command made this?
qs.x: It is labelled a merged cell. Merge Cells joins selected cells into one.

qs.q: Split Cells is used to:
o: Divide a cell into two or more cells
Join two or more cells into one
qs.x: Split Cells divides cells; Merge Cells joins them.

qs.q: The table move handle:
o: Lets you drag the table to any location in the document
qs.x: Table move handle — dragging moves the table to any location within the document.

qs.q: The small ⊕ that appears between rows on the left edge of a table, used to add a row quickly, is the:
qs.x: The lecture labels it the Insert control.

qs.q: Insert Above, Insert Below, Insert Left and Insert Right are in which group of the Table Tools Layout tab?
qs.x: Rows & Columns group: Delete, Insert Above/Below/Left/Right.

qs.q: Which tool on the Table Tools Layout tab removes gridlines between cells?
qs.x: The Draw group has Draw Table and Eraser (erase gridlines).

qs.q: Sort, Repeat Header Rows, Convert to Text and Formula are found in which group of the Table Tools Layout tab?
qs.x: These sit in the Data group.

qs.q: Text Direction and Cell Margins are in which group of the Table Tools Layout tab?
qs.x: The Alignment group: align text within a cell, Text Direction, Cell Margins.

qs.q: Distribute Rows makes:
o: All selected rows the same height
qs.x: Distribute Rows evens the row heights; Distribute Columns evens column widths (Cell Size group).

qs.q: The Table Styles gallery is on the Table Tools ______ tab.
qs.x: Formatting a Table (1 of 3) shows the gallery on the Table Tools Design tab.

qs.q: The Table Styles gallery groups its styles into:
o: Plain Tables, Grid Tables and List Tables
qs.x: Plain Table styles, Grid Table styles, and (scroll) List styles.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a Table Style Option check box?
qs.x: Table Style Options: Header Row, First Column, Total Row, Last Column, Banded Rows, Banded Columns.

qs.q: Table alignment is:
o: The horizontal position of a table between the left and right document margins
The alignment of text inside each cell
The direction of text in a cell
qs.x: That is the lecture's definition of table alignment.

qs.q: When you first insert a table, it aligns at the:
qs.x: An inserted table aligns at the left margin. You can centre it or align it right.

qs.q: According to the lecture, table text is:
o: Formatted just as any other text
qs.x: Table text — formatted just as any other text.

qs.q: In the Table Properties dialog box, the two text-wrapping options for a table are:
qs.x: Text wrapping: None or Around (wrap text around a selected table).

qs.q: The Borders and Shading dialog box has which three tabs?
qs.x: Borders and Shading dialog: Borders, Page Border, Shading tabs.

qs.q: In the Borders tab, which is NOT a border Setting?
qs.x: Settings: None, Box, All, Grid, Custom.

qs.q: When converting text to a table, which is NOT a "Separate text at" option?
qs.x: Separate text at: Paragraphs, Commas, Tabs, Other.

qs.q: In the Convert Text to Table example, each line has a description, a tab, then a number of jobs. How many columns does the table get?
qs.x: Number of columns: 2 (one tab per line splits each line into two pieces).

qs.q: When converting a table to text, the text can be separated with:
o: Paragraph marks, Tabs, Commas or Other
qs.x: Convert Table To Text: Paragraph marks, Tabs, Commas, Other.

qs.q: Mail merge is used to:
o: Send the same personalized document to a number of people
Merge two Word documents into one file
Join several table cells into one
qs.x: Mail Merge sends the same personalized document to a number of people.

qs.q: A typical example of a mail merge document is a:
qs.x: The lecture's example: form letter.

qs.q: Mail merge is a process that combines content from:
o: A main document and a data source
A template and a cover page
qs.x: Mail merge combines a main document and a data source.

qs.q: In a mail merge, the main document contains:
o: Wording that remains the same for all recipients
The list of names and addresses
qs.x: Main document — wording that remains the same for all recipients.

qs.q: In a mail merge, the data source is:
o: A list of variable data included in the document
The wording that stays the same
The printer used for the merge
qs.x: Data source — list of variable data included in the document.

qs.q: Each item of information in a data source, such as Last name, is a:
qs.x: Field — each item of information in the data source.

qs.q: A group of fields for one person or thing, shown as a ROW, is a:
qs.x: Record — group of fields for a person or thing, represented as a row.

qs.q: In a data source shown as a worksheet, the COLUMNS are the ______ and the ROWS are the ______.
qs.x: Columns (fields), rows containing records. The first row is the header row with the field names.

qs.q: The first row of a data source, which contains the field names (LastName, FirstName, Street…), is the:
qs.x: Fields and Header row: the header row contains field names.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a data source for a mail merge?
qs.x: Data sources: Word document, Access table or query, Excel worksheet, Outlook contacts.

qs.q: Mail merge commands are found on the ______ tab.
qs.x: Start Mail Merge, Select Recipients and Finish & Merge are on the Mailings tab.

qs.q: Which option is NOT on the Select Recipients menu?
qs.x: Select Recipients: Type a New List, Use an Existing List, Choose from Outlook Contacts. Validate addresses is in the Recipients dialog.

qs.q: You already have your recipients' details saved in an Excel file. On the Select Recipients menu you choose:
qs.x: Use an Existing List picks an existing file such as Address List.xlsx.

qs.q: In the Mail Merge Recipients dialog box, unticking the check box next to a name:
o: Removes that recipient from the merge
Deletes the person from the Excel file
qs.x: Use the checkboxes to add or remove recipients from the merge.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a "Refine recipient list" option in the Mail Merge Recipients dialog box?
qs.x: Refine recipient list: Sort, Filter, Find duplicates, Find recipient, Validate addresses.

qs.q: In the Mail Merge Recipients dialog box, the Edit button lets you:
qs.x: Edit… → Edit records.

qs.q: «AddressBlock» and «GreetingLine» in the letter are:
o: Merge fields placed in the document
qs.x: Merge fields placed in the document (Write & Insert Fields group).

qs.q: The final step that produces the personalized letters is:
qs.x: Finish & Merge completes the mail merge.

qs.q: In the lecture's address list (Carden, Crawford, Dugan, Finnegan, Madison, Morgan, Slater, Smith), how many records are there?
qs.x: Rows 2 to 9 hold 8 records; row 1 is the header row.

qs.q: In the lecture's address list, how many fields does each record have?
qs.x: LastName, FirstName, Street, City, State, Zip, Fax = 7 fields.

qs.q: An electronic form is:
o: A structured document that is completed electronically
A letter sent to many people
A list of figures in a document
A document that creates a copy of itself
qs.x: Electronic form: a structured document that is completed electronically.

qs.q: Content controls for building an electronic form are found on the ______ tab.
qs.x: The Electronic Form slide shows the Controls group on the Developer tab.

qs.q: Which content control lets the user enter a large amount of text, even several paragraphs, that can be formatted and include images and tables?
qs.x: Rich Text — large amount of formatted text, even with images and tables.

qs.q: Which content control holds text or numbers that can be read by any text editor, with limited formatting?
qs.x: Plain Text — readable by any text or file editor; limited formatting.

qs.q: Which content control inserts a reusable piece of content such as a header or disclaimer?
qs.x: Building Block Gallery — a piece of content designed to be used multiple times.

qs.q: Which content control lets the user select or deselect an item by clicking beside it?
qs.x: Check Box — select or deselect an item.

qs.q: Which content control shows a list of items but ALSO lets the user type their own entry?
qs.x: Combo Box combines a text box with a list box.

qs.q: Which content control only allows the user to choose from a predefined list of choices?
qs.x: Drop-Down List — select from a predefined list. (A Combo Box also lets you type.)

qs.q: Which content control lets the user select a date from a calendar?
qs.x: Date Picker — select a date from a calendar.

qs.q: Which content control is designed to repeat content, often including other content controls, inside a single control?
qs.x: Repeating Section.

qs.q: Which content control would you use for a passport-size photo on an application form?
qs.x: Picture — insert a picture in a field.

qs.q: "Click or tap here to enter text" shown in an empty form field is called:
qs.x: The lecture labels it instructional text.

qs.q: On the Developer tab, Properties is greyed out because:
qs.x: Properties is grayed because a content control is not selected.

qs.q: Features for academic documents (ToC, footnotes, citations) are accessed through the ______ tab.
qs.x: Can be accessed through the References tab.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the academic document features listed in the lecture?
qs.x: The four: Table of Contents, Table of Figures, Footnotes and Endnotes, Citations/Bibliography.

qs.q: An automatically generated Table of Contents is useful because:
o: Its page numbers readjust automatically when the document grows or shrinks
It lists every figure in the document
qs.x: Page numbers in an automatic ToC readjust when the document grows/shrinks.

qs.q: A Table of Figures lets you:
o: List and organize the figures, pictures or tables in your document
List the headings of the document
qs.x: ToF lists and organizes figures, pictures or tables, much like a table of contents.

qs.q: Before Word can build a Table of Figures automatically, each figure needs a:
qs.x: The ToF slide goes from Insert Caption → Caption dialog → "Figure 1: Action Research Spiral".

qs.q: In the Caption dialog box, which setting is chosen in the lecture example for where the caption goes?
o: At the end of the document
qs.x: Position: Below selected item.

qs.q: In the Caption dialog box, the Label option lets you choose:
o: Figure, Table or a new label
qs.x: Label: Figure (with New Label… to add your own).

qs.q: If a Table of Figures is generated automatically, its page numbers:
o: Are readjusted automatically when the document grows or shrinks
qs.x: ToF (2 of 2): page numbers readjust automatically.

qs.q: A style manual is:
o: A set of rules and standards for writing documents
A list of sources at the end of a document
qs.x: Style manual — set of rules and standards for writing documents.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a setting a style manual suggests, according to the lecture?
qs.x: Style manuals cover margins, line & paragraph spacing, footnotes/endnotes, citation of sources and bibliography.

qs.q: According to the lecture, sources are used to:
qs.x: Sources — supplement your own thoughts.

qs.q: Stealing and passing off the ideas or words of another person as your own is called:
qs.x: Plagiarizing.

qs.q: A writing style is:
o: A set of rules that results in standardized documents
A font such as Times New Roman
qs.x: Writing style — set of rules that results in standardized documents.

qs.q: The writing style normally used in the HUMANITIES disciplines is:
qs.x: Humanities — MLA (Modern Language Association).

qs.q: The writing style used in business, economics, communication and social sciences is:
qs.x: APA (American Psychological Association).

qs.q: Which writing style is associated with the preparation of papers and books?
qs.x: Preparation of papers and books — Chicago.

qs.q: Which writing style is used for history papers?
qs.x: The slide says history papers — Turabian style.

qs.q: MLA stands for:
qs.x: MLA (Modern Language Association).

qs.q: APA stands for:
qs.x: APA (American Psychological Association).

qs.q: Where do you choose the writing style (e.g. MLA, APA) in Word?
o: The Style arrow in the Citations & Bibliography group on the References tab
The Styles group on the Home tab
qs.x: References → Citations & Bibliography → Style arrow.

qs.q: To add a new source to your document, you click:
o: Insert Citation, then Add New Source
qs.x: First add each source: click Insert Citation → select Add New Source.

qs.q: In the Create Source dialog box, the first thing you choose is the:
qs.x: Type of Source, then Author, Title, Journal Name, Year, Pages.

qs.q: On the Insert Citation menu, Add New Placeholder lets you:
o: Mark where a citation goes now and fill in the source details later
Copy a source to the Master List
qs.x: A placeholder source is marked with ? in the Source Manager until you complete it.

qs.q: In the Source Manager, the Master List contains:
o: Sources available to all documents on the computer
Only the sources in the current document
qs.x: Master List = sources available to all documents on a computer; Current List = sources available in the current document.

qs.q: In the Source Manager's Current List, a ✓ beside a source means it is a:
qs.x: ✓ cited source, ? placeholder source.

qs.q: The Source Manager dialog box opens when you click:
qs.x: Manage Sources opens the Source Manager (search box, Copy, Delete, Edit, New).

qs.q: "Hayes (2011) has identified two principles that are essential for transferability." This is an example of:
o: Citing a source in your document
qs.x: Make reference to any of the sources by citing it in your document.

qs.q: A bibliography:
o: Lists all the sources cited in the document
Lists all the headings with page numbers
qs.x: Bibliography: add a bibliography, which lists all the sources cited in the document.

qs.q: To generate a bibliography, you:
o: Place the cursor where the bibliography should go, then click Bibliography
Click Insert Footnote at the end of the document
qs.x: Generating Bibliography: place cursor → click Bibliography.

qs.q: In the lecture's sample bibliography (Abbott, Archer, Bishop, Checkland…), the entries are arranged:
o: In the order they were cited
qs.x: Abbott → Archer → Bishop → Checkland → Craig → Denbow → Hayes → Hosman → Koshy → McIntyre.

qs.q: Footnotes and endnotes are used for:
o: References and elaborations/explanations of points raised in the main text
qs.x: Used for: references; elaborations/explanations of points raised in the main text.

qs.q: A footnote is a note placed at the:
qs.x: Footnotes: notes at the end of the page.

qs.q: An endnote is a note placed at the:
qs.x: Endnotes: notes at the end of the document.

qs.q: Footnotes and endnotes are both automatically numbered with:
qs.x: Both are automatically numbered with superscripts.

qs.q: By default, footnote numbering starts from:
qs.x: Footnotes: start from 1.

qs.q: By default, endnote numbering starts from:
qs.x: Endnotes: start from Roman numeral i.

qs.q: Before inserting a footnote, you move the cursor:
o: To the right of the text where you want the footnote
To the end of the document
qs.x: Move to the right of the text where you want to insert the footnote or endnote.

qs.q: Insert Footnote and Insert Endnote are found in the Footnotes group on the ______ tab.
qs.x: References tab, Footnotes group.

qs.q: The Next Footnote button lets you:
o: Move from one note to the next within the document
qs.x: Move from one note to the next within the document.

qs.q: The Show Notes button:
o: Shows the location of the notes at the end of the page or document
qs.x: Shows location of note at end of page or document.

qs.q: To delete a footnote, you:
o: Highlight the note reference within the text and press Delete
Delete the note text at the bottom of the page only
qs.x: Deleting footnote: highlight note to delete within text → press Delete.

qs.q: In the lecture example, the superscript 1 after "world's population" links to the note "43% according to UNFPA (2011)" at the bottom of the page. This note is a:
qs.x: It sits at the end of the page, so it is a footnote.

sets.title: Question bank drill
sets.desc: 207 questions from the Lecture 1–3 question bank and extras.

qs.q: What is Information?
o: Properly kept documents in any institution
qs.x: Data = raw facts; information = data that has been processed into a usable form.

qs.q: What is software?
o: A set of instructions that direct a computer's hardware to perform a task
Computer information that has been processed by computer instructions
Data that has been processed and is ready to be used in decision making
Output generated by a central processing unit
qs.x: Software is the set of instructions; hardware is the physical parts that obey them.

qs.q: What term is used to refer to the set of instructions that directs the computer hardware to accomplish a task?
qs.x: Same idea worded differently: instructions directing hardware = software.

qs.q: What are the two types of software?
qs.x: Lecture 1: software is either system software or application software.

qs.q: Which Software helps a computer perform essential operating tasks and enables other software to run?
qs.x: System software runs the machine and lets application software work on top of it.

qs.q: Which of the following are examples of system software programs?
qs.x: Mac OS and UNIX are operating systems, i.e. system software. MS Office is application software.

qs.q: Which software allows the application software to interact with the computer?
qs.x: System software sits between the application and the hardware.

qs.q: What does system software include?
o: Operating systems, translators and utilities that enable the computer to function
Generic application programs and operating systems that control the resources of a computer
Operating systems, translators and applications that enable the computer to function
System Utilities and integrated application packages that manage the resources of a computer
qs.x: System software = operating systems, translators (compilers) and utilities.

qs.q: Which is the first program to run on a computer when the computer boots up?
qs.x: The operating system loads first at boot; everything else runs on top of it.

qs.q: The basic operations of a computer are managed by the___
qs.x: The OS manages input, processing, storage and output for you.

qs.q: Which of the following primarily manages a computers resources?
qs.x: Managing processor, memory, storage and devices is the OS's job.

qs.q: What software controls the operations and activities of a computer and its devices?
qs.x: The OS controls the operations and activities of the computer and its devices.

qs.q: What type of software category does Windows XP fall under?
qs.x: Windows XP is an operating system, so it is system software.

qs.q: Which of the following tasks is NOT performed by an operating system?
qs.x: Word processing is an application task, not an operating-system task.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of an OS?
qs.x: Windows Explorer is a file manager that runs on Windows; it is not an OS.

qs.q: Which of the following criteria explains why computer systems have been adopted in business?
o: Speed, accuracy, and large storage capacity
Never disappoints, large storage and big
Thinking, never tired and cost effective
Speed, high IQ, accuracy and smart
qs.x: Lecture 1 'Benefits': computers are fast, accurate and store huge amounts of data.

qs.q: Which of the following criteria best describes a computer as being powerful?
o: Speed, accuracy and large storage capacity
Speed, high IQ, accuracy and smart
Thinking, never tired and cost effective
Never disappoints, large storage and big
qs.x: Same benefits list: speed, accuracy and large storage capacity.

qs.q: Which of the following is the correct order of data processing cycle?
qs.x: The information processing cycle: input, then processing, then output.

qs.q: Which of the following shows a sequence of the stages in the processing cycle?
qs.x: With storage added, the full cycle is input, processing, output, storage.

qs.q: Which of the following is not a means by which data is input into the computer?
qs.x: A monitor is an output device; keyboard, mouse and microphone are inputs.

qs.q: What are the devices that translate information processed by the computer into a form that humans can understand called?
qs.x: Output hardware turns processed data into a form humans can understand.

qs.q: Which device uses light-sensing (optical) equipment to convert images of text, drawings, and photos into digital form?
qs.x: A scanner uses light-sensing (optical) equipment to digitise text and images.

qs.q: Which of these devices can be used to transfer a hardcopy document or graphic image to a digitalized format?
qs.x: A scanner converts a hardcopy document into digital form.

qs.q: Which of the following is an alternative to a mouse in laptop computers?
qs.x: A trackball is a pointing device used in place of a mouse.

qs.q: Keys found on the top or the left of the keyboard that are used to execute commands specific to the software being used are called?
qs.x: F1-F12 (and side keys) are function keys that run software-specific commands.

qs.q: In order to play and hear music from a computer what does one need?
qs.x: To hear sound you need a sound card plus speakers (output).

qs.q: In order to record music on a computer what does one need?
qs.x: To record sound you need a sound card plus a microphone (input).
